episode_title: Repulsion-driven superconductivity in twisted MoTe2, magnetorotons beyond Landau levels, and a Dirac spin liquid verdict

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: It's November 4th, and the arXiv dumped about forty-eight condensed matter papers overnight. We're not doing all of them.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Thankfully. Today's got a DMRG study that actually finds topological superconductivity in twisted moly-telluride from pure repulsion, a coupled-wire theory of magnetorotons that reaches past the Landau level, and a neural-network verdict on the thirty-year-old kagome spin liquid question. Plus two papers on rhombohedral graphene optics and transport.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Let's start with the M-o-T-e-two paper, since that's the one closest to what's actually happening on a chip right now. Show notes number one, Wang, Soejima, and collaborators including Vishwanath and Zaletel.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, so the backstory: experiments last year or so found superconductivity in twisted bilayer M-o-T-e-two right next to a fractional Chern insulator at filling minus two-thirds, with no magnetic field. Ferromagnetic, so no plain s-wave pairing allowed. Everyone's been asking whether you can get superconductivity out of a purely repulsive microscopic model of this material, not some idealized flat-band toy.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And that's the hard part — idealized models with uniform quantum geometry or no periodic potential had already shown chiral f-wave pairing. But the real moiré band has both a periodic potential and non-uniform quantum geometry. So does the real thing still pair?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They project gate-screened Coulomb interactions into the single narrow Chern band from a realistic continuum model, twist angle three point eight nine degrees, and run infinite DMRG on cylinders of circumference four to seven moiré unit cells. They track Cooper-pair correlations along the cylinder.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: On a quasi-one-D cylinder you can't spontaneously break charge symmetry, so superconductivity shows up as a Luther-Emery liquid — power-law pair correlations instead of true long-range order.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the key check is whether that power law gets stronger as the cylinder gets fatter. They find the exponent drops from about one point seven at six unit cells around to one point three at seven, consistent with flowing toward a genuine two-dimensional superconductor as circumference grows.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: What's the pairing symmetry?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They measure a proxy pair wavefunction in momentum space and its phase winds six pi around the Fermi surface — angular momentum minus three, chiral f-wave. Combined with the Chern number of the band, that predicts an odd number of chiral Majorana edge modes. They confirm it directly with a string-order correlator in the number-conserving DMRG, which shows the same algebraic decay you'd expect for non-Abelian vortices binding Majorana zero modes.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So it's not just superconducting, it's topologically non-trivial superconducting. What about actual numbers — gap, transition temperature?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Single-electron gap under half a milli-electron-volt, superfluid stiffness around thirty micro-electron-volts. Stiffness sets a BKT bound of order five hundred milli-kelvin, and that's the tighter constraint — the pair-breaking gap alone would allow kelvins. So experimentally you're stiffness-limited, not gap-limited.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the dome sits at minus point seven eight to minus point seven two filling at zero displacement field — pretty close to where the experiment actually sees it.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yes, and it extends to finite displacement field too, so it doesn't rely on the inversion symmetry present only at zero field. Nearby they map out the full cast: a metal connecting to the quantum anomalous Hall insulator at filling minus one, the fractional Chern insulator at minus two-thirds, a topological charge density wave that the FCI turns into under displacement field — and that CDW is their candidate explanation for the mysterious re-entrant integer Hall regime seen in some devices.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: What's the catch? They're pretty candid that the charge-ordered phase next to the superconductor is hard to pin down precisely.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right — away from exact two-thirds filling, the charge order should be gapless, but DMRG convergence gets rough there, so they can't nail its universality class. And the whole picture depends on screening length — superconductivity survives out to about five nanometers of effective screening but gets harder to converge as you go longer-ranged. Still, this is about as close as DMRG has gotten to deriving the observed superconducting dome from a first-principles-parameterized Hamiltonian rather than a cartoon model.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper two, show notes, is a theory piece from Emanuel and Oreg at Weizmann — collective modes of fractional states beyond Landau levels.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: This is about the magnetoroton, the famous dispersing neutral mode of fractional quantum Hall states, the one Girvin, MacDonald and Platzman worked out decades ago. It dips to a minimum at finite momentum, and gap closure there is associated with melting into a Wigner crystal. At zero momentum it becomes the chiral graviton, a spin-two excitation that's been seen in recent FQH experiments.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the open question is whether fractional Chern insulators — the zero-field, lattice cousins of the FQHE — have the same mode, given they're nowhere near the idealized lowest-Landau-level limit.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Exactly, and almost everyone who's looked at FCI magnetorotons so far has done it in the regime where the band is secretly Landau-level-like — the ideal quantum geometry limit. This paper wants an analytic handle that works away from that limit, and it reaches for coupled-wire constructions.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Worth a beat on what that is for anyone who hasn't touched it since a methods course — you replace the two-dimensional electron system with an array of one-dimensional wires, bosonize each wire, and add inter-wire tunneling terms that reproduce the Hall response. It's exactly solvable in a way genuine two-D interacting problems usually aren't.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right. In this construction, the operator that opens the Laughlin gap becomes, after a change of variables, a sine-Gordon model — solitons are the Laughlin quasiparticles and quasiholes. The new result here is that neutral collective modes — the magnetorotons — are just bound soliton-antisoliton pairs: dipoles when they sit on two different wires, give you the large-momentum part of the magnetoroton branch, and quadrupole bound states, breathers, give you the zero-momentum chiral-graviton-like mode.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And this reproduces the qualitative shape of the magnetoroton even in a maximally anisotropic wire geometry, which is itself interesting — suggests the phenomenology doesn't require rotational symmetry or Landau-level physics at all.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Then they port the whole machinery onto an actual FCI model — one built by two of the same authors previously, that can be tuned away from ideal quantum geometry via an anti-FCI competing operator. The punchline: the magnetoroton gap shrinks as the quantum metric moves away from the ideal trace-condition limit, which directly ties the geometric stability hypothesis — the idea that flatter, more ideal quantum geometry stabilizes fractional states — to an actual observable gap closure.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the chiral graviton mode's stability tracks the same trend?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yes — closer to ideal geometry also favors the long-wavelength quadrupole surviving as a sharp mode rather than decaying into a two-magnetoroton continuum. What they can't get at: the dip region itself, momenta below the magnetoroton minimum, where the excitation smoothly interpolates between dipole and quadrupole — that's inherently a continuum effect their discrete wire picture can't capture. And they're upfront that coupled-wire constructions don't give quantitative numbers, just trends — still, for anyone thinking about collective modes in twisted M-o-T-e-two or rhombohedral graphene FCIs, this is a nice analytic cross-check on what numerics have been finding.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Switching fields entirely — paper three is a machine-learning assault on the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet, by Sun, Roth, Chen and Heyl.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: This is the classic unsolved spin-liquid problem — spin-half Heisenberg model on the kagome lattice, candidate ground state for herbertsmithite and friends. DMRG on cylinders hinted at a gapped Z2 spin liquid, then at something gapless; variational Monte Carlo with Gutzwiller-projected parton wavefunctions keeps finding a U one Dirac spin liquid and a competing Z2 state nearly tied in energy. Nobody's settled it.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And there was a recent neural-network paper claiming a totally different answer — a spinon pair-density-wave state — which is the backdrop here.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, and this paper's first job is basically forensic: they build a geometry-aware convolutional network, KagomeResNet, that does message-passing directly along the kagome bonds rather than on a generic grid, get the lowest variational energies reported for this model on tori up to three hundred spins, and then show the earlier claim doesn't reproduce. Their Monte Carlo acceptance rate stays healthy around fifty-five percent — the giveaway for the earlier result was non-ergodic sampling that artificially lowered the energy and shifted the apparent ground-state quantum numbers.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So no spinon pair-density wave. What positive evidence do they have for the Dirac liquid specifically?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Three independent checks. First, spin and dimer structure factors show no sign of magnetic or valence-bond order — the peaks scale to zero as the system grows. Second — and this is the elegant part — they symmetry-resolve the dominant spin and dimer correlations and find they collapse onto a single, common power-law decay, exactly what you'd expect if both operators are different components of the same emergent SO-six multiplet of monopole operators that the Dirac spin liquid's effective field theory predicts.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's a genuinely sharp test — not just 'no order,' but matching a specific predicted scaling relation between two different operators.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And third, they compute the fidelity — the wavefunction overlap — between their optimized network state and representative Gutzwiller-projected Dirac and Z2 states. The network isn't biased toward either family, so it's a fair referee. The overlap with the Dirac reference wins, and the margin grows with system size even against the most competitive Z2 candidate.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Caveat — it's still a finite-size, variational calculation, three hundred spins isn't the thermodynamic limit, and fidelity comparisons depend on which specific projected states you pick as the competitors.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: True, but as a demonstration that geometry-aware neural quantum states can out-compete decades of tensor-network and VMC efforts on a genuinely hard frustrated problem, it's a solid proof of concept — and it's a nice methodological cousin to techniques you might eventually want for correlated states in moiré systems.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Back to two dimensions people actually shine light on — paper four, chirality rules for optical vortices in rhombohedral graphene multilayers.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: This is squarely in dipole-matrix-element territory, which should feel familiar from TMD selection rules. An optical zero is a momentum where the interband dipole vanishes — dark transition — and because the dipole is a complex field, its phase winds around that zero by an integer. That integer is a topological charge of the optical response, and it controls the shift current, the main mechanism behind the bulk photovoltaic effect.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And rhombohedral — chirally stacked — graphene is a clean place to study this because the stacking order N is a single tunable integer that controls everything about the low-energy bands.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They derive this with a Löwdin downfolding of the tight-binding Hamiltonian onto the two outer sites, which organizes the effective coupling as a sum over hopping paths. From that they get four clean rules. One: the total vortex charge near the K valley, per linear polarization, is exactly N minus one, and it's conserved — trigonal warping and displacement field can redistribute it among multiple zeros but never change the sum.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: What's rule two?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Protection — for N three and above, the K point itself stays an exact dark point no matter how much you warp or bias it, because there's no direct bond connecting the two low-energy sublattices once you're past the bilayer. The Bernal bilayer is the one exception — there the skew hopping does bridge them directly, so the vortex gets expelled from K out to a finite momentum set by a simple formula involving the hopping parameters.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the other two rules?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Rule three: wherever the charge does land away from K, the satellite radii all scale linearly with the trigonal-warping strength, set by one combination of hopping parameters, regardless of N. Rule four: the amount of charge left pinned exactly at K has a clean formula in N that's independent of bias for N four and up — the trilayer is the special marginal case where bias alone decides how the degenerate charge there splits.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They also build a quantized integer staircase, I take it, to count all this directly?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, a quantity they call the interband character, vorticity minus interband Berry flux, which steps by exactly the vortex charge every time your integration disk crosses a zero. It's a nice Gauss's-law bookkeeping tool, and it survives all the remote hopping corrections they throw at it — gamma four, gamma two, the real tight-binding mess — because these are protected integers, not fitted numbers.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the physical payoff?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: The band-edge shift current itself grows linearly with N — same integer that fixes the vortex charge also sets the magnitude of the photocurrent, because it's literally the degree of the same chiral monomial in the effective Hamiltonian. The main caveat is this is all single-particle and clean-limit — they're explicit that excitonic corrections and disorder will dress the exact numbers, though they argue the integer charges themselves can't be moved by any smooth renormalization.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Last deep dive, paper five, stays with rhombohedral graphene but swaps optics for the anomalous Hall effect — Bi and Varma.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: The motivating puzzle: rhombohedral graphene shows a robust anomalous Hall effect in its valley-polarized quarter-metal states, and the obvious reference point is Haldane's model, where a quantized Hall response comes with equilibrium circulating bond currents breaking time reversal locally. Do the graphene states actually have those loop currents?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the answer is no, which is the headline.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They work directly in real space with the full eight-band tight-binding model for ABCA tetralayer graphene. First they show analytically that in the uniform valley-polarized state, every bond current vanishes exactly — there's a combined mirror-and-time-reversal symmetry that pins it to zero even though the state itself isn't time-reversal symmetric. So the Hall effect here is not a Haldane-type loop-current state.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Then where does the Hall response actually come from, if not real circulating currents?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: From interference between different electron propagation paths in the current-current correlation function — closed products of hopping amplitudes that form what they call Wilson loops. Because the two valleys carry opposite Berry curvature but unequal occupation once you're valley-polarized, the cross terms between forward and backward paths around these loops don't cancel, and that imbalance is the Hall signal.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's a nice real-space translation of something normally only discussed as a Berry-curvature integral in momentum space.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, and they make it quantitative — the charge in this system lives mostly on the top and bottom layers, so they do a Löwdin-style surface projection down to just those two sites, building up successive approximations with different combinations of hoppings. Keeping the direct intralayer and vertical dimer hoppings plus the same-sublattice remote hopping gets them within point two percent of the full eight-band Hall conductivity.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So a genuinely minimal real-space model captures almost all of the effect.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And as a bonus prediction, they show that a smooth local potential — a gate bump, or a screened charged impurity — does generate real equilibrium circulating currents around the defect, with a strength set by both the Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment of the states at the Fermi surface. They compute the resulting stray magnetic field profile, which is directly comparable to nanoSQUID measurements already being done on these samples. Main limitation: they assume full, rigid spin-valley polarization everywhere, no self-consistent screening of the added potential, so near a domain wall or defect this picture would need to be redone self-consistently.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Good set of quick ones to close out. Paper six — strained graphene, flat bands from periodic deformation.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Tight-binding calculations showing that if you twist the periodic strain pattern relative to the atomic lattice, you kill the band flattening that periodic strain is supposed to produce — so alignment between the two lattices is essential, and the flattening itself is controlled by a single pseudo-magnetic-field-flux parameter. Useful cautionary note for anyone chasing strain-engineered flat bands as a correlated-electron platform.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper seven, Kekulé graphene superlattices and a valley diode.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: A tunnel junction in a Kekulé-patterned graphene superlattice can carry a valley-polarized supercurrent-like flow that's strongly nonreciprocal — forward and backward valley currents differ — even with no actual superconductivity involved. The mechanism is just an extra reflection phase picked up per transverse channel, and the authors get up to one hundred percent rectification efficiency, gate-tunable. A dissipationless valleytronics proposal, purely theoretical for now.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper eight is a formal one — torsion and Berry phases around dislocations in graphene.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They work out the geometric phase a quasiparticle picks up encircling a lattice dislocation, treating it via Katanaev-Volovich torsion confined to the defect core. Isolated dislocations get a topological valley phase depending on whether the Burgers vector sits outside the root-three superlattice, following a three-coloring rule based on which sites the pentagon and heptagon defects sit on. Nice formal unification of several known special cases, including why a five-eight-five defect core can look invisible or carry a definite flux depending on exactly how it's constructed.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper nine — isolating the quantum metric from Berry curvature using semi-Dirac semimetals.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: At a special chiral point of type-two semi-Dirac semimetals, chiral and PT symmetry together kill the Berry curvature, its dipole, and the shift current entirely, leaving the quantum metric and its dipole as the only source of the optical and nonlinear Hall response. That gives a clean experimental fingerprint — a divergent longitudinal optical conductivity and a singular nonlinear Hall response right at the band touching — and turning on the spin-orbit mass parameter switches the Berry-curvature channels back on, letting you disentangle the two types of quantum geometry by their different relaxation-time scaling.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And last, paper ten, back to real materials — scanning tunneling spectroscopy on monolayer iron selenide on strontium titanate.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: This interface famously superconducts at nearly ten times bulk iron selenide's transition temperature, but the tunneling spectra never show clean coherence peaks, so the gap size has stayed ambiguous. By tracking how the tunneling current decays with tip height across different bias voltages, they separate Andreev-reflection-dominated tunneling below six milli-electron-volts from quasiparticle-dominated tunneling above thirteen, with a mixed regime in between — pinning the superconducting gap to that six-to-thirteen window using pure statistics rather than peak-fitting.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's today's set. A lot of moiré and graphene theory, one neural-network referee call on a thirty-year-old spin liquid debate, and an actual gap measurement on a real sample to ground it all.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Enough for one morning. See you tomorrow.

picks.title: Repulsion-Driven Topological Superconductivity in Twisted MoTe2
picks.abstract: We show that a microscopic model of twisted MoTe2 with screened Coulomb interactions produces topological superconductivity. Using the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) on infinite cylinders, we find that the narrow Chern band of twisted MoTe2 has Cooper pair correlations that strengthen with cylinder circumference, consistent with two dimensional superconductivity. The superconductor has chiral f-wave pairing around the valley center, and its topology produces chiral Majorana edge modes and non-Abelian vortex cores. At zero displacement field, the superconductor spans fillings -0.78\lesssim\nu\lesssim-0.72, close to the experimental range, and extends in a dome to finite displacement field. We then predict how its stiffness evolves with the filling and the tunable displacement field. The interplay with screening length is also examined. Nearby, we find a fractional Chern insulator, a topological charge density wave, a metal, and a charge-ordered state. The last is a candidate for the reentrant integer Hall regime in experiments. These results establish a route from repulsive interactions in microscopic models of moiré materials to chiral topological uperconductors with chiral Majorana edge modes.
picks.why: DMRG evidence for repulsion-driven chiral f-wave topological superconductivity with Majorana edge modes in twisted MoTe2 directly addresses the correlated-state physics of moiré TMDs central to the profile.

picks.title: Collective Modes of Fractional States Beyond Landau Levels
picks.abstract: Collective modes provide a powerful probe into the properties and stability of topologically ordered and strongly interacting phases of matter, such as fractional quantum Hall states. Yet, the description of fractional-state excitations away from the Landau-level limit remains a formidable challenge. We develop a framework for describing collective excitations in the strong-coupling regime of coupled-wire constructions and show that they emerge as solitons and breathers of effective sine-Gordon theories. This approach provides a systematic route to studying collective modes in a broad class of fractional states. Applied to a coupled-wire construction of the fractional quantum Hall effect, the framework captures key features of the magnetoroton branch. It naturally extends to fractional Chern insulators, demonstrating that magnetoroton-like collective modes persist well beyond the Landau-level limit. We find that the magnetoroton gap increases as the Fubini-Study metric approaches the ideal (trace-condition) limit, highlighting the important role of quantum geometry in the stability of fractionalized phases and their collective excitations. The same trend favors the stability of the long-wavelength quadrupolar mode associated with the chiral graviton. Together, these results identify a distinct interplay between fractionalization and quantum geometry, and provide an analytical framework for studies of collective excitations in fractional topological matter.
picks.why: A new sine-Gordon/coupled-wire framework for collective magnetoroton modes beyond Landau levels links quantum geometry to the stability of fractional Chern insulators and FQH states, core to the quantum Hall/FCI secondary interest.

picks.title: Evidence for a Dirac Spin Liquid in the Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet from High-Precision Neural-Network Quantum States
picks.abstract: The spin-1/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet is a central model in the study of quantum spin liquids, yet its ground-state properties remain unresolved. We perform large-scale variational Monte-Carlo calculations using neural-network quantum states (NQSs) with kagome-geometry-aware message-passing convolution on two-dimensional tori containing up to 300 spins, and achieve exceptionally low variational energies for the kagome model. The spin and dimer structure factors show no evidence of magnetic or valence-bond long-range order. Moreover, the dominant symmetry-resolved spin and dimer correlations exhibit a common scaling behavior consistent with the emergent SO(6) monopole multiplet of the Dirac spin liquid. Finally, the fidelity of the optimized NQSs with Gutzwiller-projected mean-field states increasingly favors the Dirac state over the competing Z2 candidates as the system size grows. Together, these complementary results provide evidence for a U(1) Dirac spin-liquid ground state in the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet.
picks.why: State-of-the-art neural-network quantum state calculations provide strong new evidence for a U(1) Dirac spin liquid ground state in the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet, a landmark result for quantum spin liquid physics broadly.

picks.title: Chirality rules for optical vortices in rhombohedral graphene multilayers
picks.abstract: Optical zeros are momenta where the interband dipole vanishes. The dipole phase winds around each of them by an integer, so they are vortices of the resonant optical response with a conserved charge. We show that in rhombohedral graphene multilayers one integer, the stacking chirality N, fixes their constellation near the K valley: the total charge per linear polarization is N-1 and is conserved under trigonal warping and interlayer bias; for N\ge3 the K point stays an exact optical zero, the Bernal bilayer being the only exception; warping places the remaining charge on satellites whose radii scale linearly with the warping; and the charge pinned at K is bias independent for N\ge4. A quantized interband character counts the enclosed charge as an integer staircase with steps at these radii, and an interlayer bias drives a satellite through the protected K vortex in the trilayer. The rules survive the remote hoppings of the full tight-binding model and, being integer charges, the corrections that reshape the bands. The same integer sets the magnitude of the response: the band-edge shift current grows linearly with N.
picks.why: Identifies universal 'chirality rules' governing optical vortices and interband dipole zeros in rhombohedral graphene multilayers, a direct optical-response result on a 2D material system closely related to the group's spectroscopy focus.

picks.title: Anomalous Hall Response and Real-Space Current Correlations in Rhombohedral Graphene
picks.abstract: We investigate the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) and magnetization observed in rhombohedral graphene through real-space calculations which lead to new insights. Our calculations reveal no equilibrium loop currents of the type associated with the Haldane model of a quantum anomalous Hall insulator. Instead, the AHE arises in this instance from interference between electronic paths forming oriented closed Wilson loops of current operators in the presence of valley polarization. We show some examples of these Wilson loops. Using the fact that the added-carrier charge density resides dominantly in the top and bottom layers, we develop a real-space expansion of the surface Hamiltonian that reproduces the Hall response of the full model with good accuracy. We also predict that a smooth local potential induces equilibrium circulating currents whose strength depends on both Berry curvature and the orbital moments of states at the Fermi surface.
picks.why: Real-space Wilson-loop analysis reframes the anomalous Hall effect in rhombohedral graphene as arising from valley-polarized current interference rather than Haldane-type loop currents, offering new microscopic insight into correlated graphene multilayer states.

picks.title: Twisting the pseudo-magnetic field lattice in periodically strained Graphene
picks.abstract: Periodic deformations flatten electronic bands of graphene which could host strongly correlated electrons similar to those observed in twisted graphene bilayers. The most spectacular effects of strong correlations like superconductivity or magnetism have however not yet been observed despite several experimental attempts. Here, we use tight-binding calculations to investigate the effect of twisting the periodic strain lattice with respect to the atomic lattice. We find that misaligning the two lattices kills the band flattening. We also report on the universal behavior of the band flattening by periodic strain which is controlled by a single parameter, a pseudo-magnetic field flux. Our study strongly suggests that controlling the twist of the strain lattice is essential to unlock the potential of periodic strains in graphene.
picks.why: Tight-binding study shows that twist-misalignment between a periodic strain pattern and the graphene lattice destroys band flattening, clarifying a key experimental knob for engineering correlated flat-band states via strain.

picks.title: Dissipationless valley diode effects in Kekulé graphene superlattices
picks.abstract: Superconducting diodes have attracted considerable interest for nonreciprocal device applications owing to their dissipationless transport. Here, we theoretically propose that a tunnel junction based on the Kekulé graphene superlattice can host a finite valley supercurrent that exhibits pronounced nonreciprocity even in the absence of superconductivity, giving rise to a dissipationless valley diode effect. This effect originates from the additional reflection phase acquired by electrons in each transverse channel and supports perfect valley diode rectification with 100\% efficiency, which can be readily tuned via the gate voltage. This finding provides a platform for designing dissipationless valleytronics in a more versatile manner.
picks.why: Proposes a dissipationless, gate-tunable valley diode effect in Kekulé graphene superlattices with 100% rectification efficiency, relevant to valleytronics in engineered graphene lattices.

picks.title: Torsion, valley holonomy, and Berry phases of quasiparticles encircling dislocations and defect complexes in graphene
picks.abstract: We investigate the geometric phase acquired by low-energy quasiparticles encircling defects in graphene. Following Anandan, this phase is the holonomy of the Poincare connection; its translational part couples momentum to torsion, giving Pa\int Ta. In the Katanaev-Volovich theory, dislocation torsion is confined to the defect core. For graphene, the relevant momentum is \hbar(\tau3\KK+\mathbf q). We show that an isolated dislocation yields a topological valley factor e\mp2\pi i/3 when its Burgers vector \bb lies outside the \sqrt3\times\sqrt3 superlattice, together with a dispersive factor e-i\mathbf q\cdot\bb for every nonzero \bb. The topological factor recovers the lattice result of Mesaros et al. as a torsion-flux phase; 4-8 dislocations retain only the dispersive contribution. Composing Volterra elements gives the holonomy of defect complexes. At zero net Frank angle, it depends only on the net Burgers vector. The valley flux obeys a three-coloring rule: pentagons and heptagons contribute according to their Kekule site color, whereas squares and octagons do not. Atomic models confirm that ring content alone does not fix the phase: a 5-8-5 core is invisible as a divacancy or as a dislocation with |\bb|=\sqrt3a, but carries flux \pm1/3 for \bb=2\mathbf a1. The torsion trace produces no geometric phase: its vector coupling violates time-reversal symmetry, while the allowed axial coupling causes only anisotropic short-range scattering.
picks.why: Derives how lattice dislocations and defect complexes in graphene produce quantized valley Berry-phase holonomies, connecting torsion/defect geometry to valley physics.

picks.title: Symmetry-protected isolation of the quantum metric in chiral type-II semi-Dirac semimetals
picks.abstract: Quantum geometry, comprising the Berry curvature (BC) and the quantum metric (QM), underpins a wide array of topological and transport phenomena. However, in most solid-state platforms, BC and QM signals are inherently entangled, making their experimental separation highly challenging. Here, we demonstrate that the chiral limit of type-II semi-Dirac semimetals provides a symmetry-protected mechanism to cleanly isolate the QM. At the chiral limit where the spin-orbit gap mz=0, chiral and \mathcalPT symmetries strictly suppress the BC, its dipole (BCD), and the shift current, leaving the QM and its dipole (QMD) as the sole sources of the optical and nonlinear Hall responses. This pure-QM regime exhibits distinct experimental fingerprints, including a divergent longitudinal optical conductivity and a QMD-induced nonlinear Hall conductivity that exhibits a pronounced singularity as the chemical potential approaches the nodal point. Turning on a finite mz reactivates the BC channels, transitioning the system from a pure-QM phase into a mixed geometric phase. By deriving a scaling law for the nonlinear Hall conductivity, we establish a direct experimental strategy to separate the mixed Drude, BCD, and QMD contributions based on their distinct relaxation-time dependencies. Our findings identify chiral type-II semi-Dirac semimetals as highly tunable platforms for isolating and probing intrinsic quantum geometric effects.
picks.why: Shows that chiral type-II semi-Dirac semimetals allow clean experimental isolation of the quantum metric from Berry curvature via nonlinear optical responses, relevant to quantum-geometry probes used in moiré/Chern band physics.

picks.title: Constraining the Superconducting Gap of Monolayer FeSe/SrTiO3 via Statistical Analysis and Tip-Height-Dependent Tunneling Spectroscopy
picks.abstract: Monolayer FeSe grown on SrTiO3 (001) exemplifies interface-enhanced superconductivity, exhibiting a transition temperature nearly ten times that of bulk FeSe. Yet, its tunneling spectra lack clearly identifiable superconducting coherence peaks, preventing an unambiguous determination of the gap magnitude. Here, we use ultralow-temperature scanning tunneling spectroscopy as a function of temperature, tip-sample separation, and lateral position to disentangle tunneling contributions by statistical analysis. Decay rates extracted by regression of tip-height-dependent spectroscopy reveal three energy regimes: Andreev-reflection-dominated tunneling below 6 meV, mixed Andreev and quasiparticle tunneling between 6 and 13 meV, and predominantly quasiparticle tunneling above 13 meV. Spatially resolved spectroscopy and correlation analysis further reveal that the tunneling conductance is predominantly localized near defects below 6 meV but becomes spatially extended at higher energies. Together, these results constrain the superconducting gap to lie between 6 and 13 meV. Our findings establish statistical analysis of spectroscopy as a powerful approach to constraining superconducting gap structures when complex spectral features prevent the unambiguous identification of coherence peaks.
picks.why: Statistical tip-height-dependent STM analysis pins down the superconducting gap (6-13 meV) of monolayer FeSe/SrTiO3, a nice methodological example of disentangling spectroscopic signatures in a 2D superconductor outside the core TMD focus.
